title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
authors: Valeria Repetto, Romina D'Aurizio, Piero Farinelli
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.

infographic.key_insight: Soft-MoQE learns input-dependent combinations of fixed quantum feature maps, avoiding quantum-parameter optimization while outperforming individual experts and simple baselines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Moving trainable routing to a classical network reduces quantum training cost by orders of magnitude in the reported benchmarks.
method: Build a heterogeneous pool of fixed, non-trainable quantum circuits.
Train a classical gating network to weight quantum embeddings for each input.
Combine expert embeddings through soft, class-dependent routing.
infographic.evidence_signal: On PCA-reduced MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST, Soft-MoQE beats the best single expert, uniform expert averaging, and a linear baseline, with task-dependent performance comparable to a trainable quantum neural network.
infographic.watch_item: Results on PCA-reduced tasks do not establish scalability or robustness on noisy quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning

title: Ising-Encoded Computational Homogenization: Stress as a Quantum Observable
authors: Mourad Halla, Suvranu De
abstract: Computational homogenization requires repeated solutions of representative volume element (RVE) problems to determine the effective response transferred to the macroscale, including the homogenized stress. Here, we develop a basis-encoded, energy-based variational quantum formulation for linear-elastic computational homogenization. The reduced finite-element energy of the RVE is expressed as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem and mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian, whose ground state represents the equilibrium fluctuation field on the encoding grid. Using the Hellmann--Feynman theorem, differentiation of the strain-dependent Hamiltonian with respect to the prescribed macroscopic strain yields stress observables whose expectation values recover the conventional volume-averaged homogenized stress. A key structural result is that, although the equilibrium Hamiltonian is two-local, the stress observables are one-local. In linear elasticity, the two-qubit coupling coefficients are independent of macroscopic strain, hence, differentiation eliminates all two-qubit coupling terms, leaving only identity and single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ operators. These observables are diagonal in the same computational basis as the Ising Hamiltonian and can therefore be evaluated from the same computational-basis measurements used for the energy. Consequently, the homogenized stress can be obtained directly from the optimized quantum state using the same computational basis measurements as the Ising Hamiltonian, without requiring reconstruction of the microscopic displacement field or an additional measurement basis. Ground states are approximated using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and the formulation is demonstrated on a two-dimensional periodic RVE.

infographic.key_insight: For linear-elastic homogenization, differentiating a two-local Ising Hamiltonian yields one-local stress observables readable from the same computational-basis measurements as the energy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation enables direct extraction of effective stress from an optimized quantum state without reconstructing microscopic displacements or adding a measurement basis.
method: Encode the reduced finite-element RVE energy as a QUBO and map it to an Ising Hamiltonian.
Approximate the equilibrium ground state using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE).
Apply Hellmann–Feynman differentiation with respect to macroscopic strain to obtain stress observables.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a demonstration on a two-dimensional periodic RVE but provides no quantitative accuracy, scaling, or hardware results.
infographic.watch_item: Stress accuracy requires validation against encoding discretization and approximate VQE convergence; the abstract establishes no quantum speedup.
infographic.paper_title: Ising-Encoded Computational Homogenization: Stress as a Quantum Observable

title: Parallel transversal entangling gates for fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computing
authors: Katrin Bolsmann, Alan Kahan, Alejandro Bermúdez, Markus Müller
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity entangling gates that can be implemented efficiently across multiple qubit pairs. We present a scheme for simultaneous pairwise entangling operations, i.e., a transversal controlled-$Z$ gate, across neighboring wells in a double-well trapped-ion architecture. A tailored dynamical decoupling scheme suppresses unwanted couplings with a pulse count that scales quadratically with the number of ions. We show that incorporating a genuine geometric cancellation reduces the pulse count and, for selected register sizes, allows the parallel operation to be completed faster than an equivalent sequence of two-qubit gates while requiring a significantly smaller two-photon Rabi frequency. We assess the experimental feasibility of the protocol by analyzing the impact of decoherence and crosstalk arising from laser wave-vector misalignment. To gain insight into the robustness of fault-tolerant protocols against realistic imperfections of the proposed transversal gate scheme, we investigate how crosstalk-induced gate errors affect the fault-tolerant preparation of a logical Bell state between two $[[4,1,2]]$ quantum-error-detection code blocks. These results highlight the potential of transversal entangling gates as a building block for trapped-ion-based scalable fault-tolerant quantum error correction.

infographic.key_insight: Parallel transversal controlled-Z gates could efficiently entangle neighboring trapped-ion registers while suppressing unwanted couplings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For selected register sizes, geometric cancellation enables faster parallel operation than sequential two-qubit gates with a substantially lower required two-photon Rabi frequency.
method: Entangle corresponding ion pairs across neighboring wells in a double-well architecture.
Suppress unwanted couplings using tailored dynamical decoupling with pulse counts scaling quadratically in ion number.
Reduce pulse overhead through geometric cancellation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study analyzes decoherence and laser-misalignment crosstalk, including their impact on fault-tolerant logical Bell-state preparation between two [[4,1,2]] code blocks.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on register size and control precision; the abstract reports feasibility analysis rather than an experimental demonstration.
infographic.paper_title: Parallel transversal entangling gates for fault-tolerant trapped-ion quantum computing

title: CAVQS: Context-Aware Variational Quantum Circuit Synthesis via Unitary Redistribution and Dynamic Reconstruction
authors: Zhilong Liu, Xiangzhen Zhou, Yunqi Huang, Xin Hong, Pengcheng Zhu, Fanxu Meng
abstract: Variational quantum circuit synthesis jointly searches circuit structure and continuous parameters to reduce costly two-qubit gates, but block-based workflows typically instantiate blocks independently, limiting simplification across block boundaries. Moreover, fully unitary synthesis does not exploit opportunities created by permitted output measurements and classical feedforward. We present CAVQS, a context-aware variational synthesis framework that combines unitary redistribution and dynamic reconstruction. First, CAVQS uses QR decomposition to transfer unitary factors between overlapping blocks, preserving the overall transformation while reshaping local synthesis targets to enable cross-block reductions. Second, for blocks that precede permitted terminal measurements, CAVQS constructs ancilla-free dynamic implementations with a CNOT-budgeted pre-measurement search and analytic branch-unitary construction, thereby minimizing expected CNOT cost. Across random-circuit targets, CAVQS reduces mean two-qubit gate counts by 28.79%-42.52%, 2.05%-52.62%, and 30.51%-74.64% relative to QFAST, SQUANDER, and Fast-USYN, respectively, on common successful instances. On 4--6-qubit quantum algorithm benchmarks, the corresponding reductions are 27.27%-36.77%, 20.65%-69.10%, and 36.31%-71.88%, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: CAVQS reduces two-qubit gate counts by optimizing across circuit-block boundaries and exploiting permitted terminal measurements with classical feedforward.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lower CNOT costs could ease hardware execution, while dynamic implementations require measurement and feedforward support.
method: Use QR decomposition to redistribute unitary factors across overlapping blocks while preserving the overall transformation.
Resynthesize context-adjusted blocks to enable cross-block gate reductions.
For eligible terminal-measurement blocks, combine CNOT-budgeted search with analytic branch unitaries to minimize expected CNOT cost without ancillas.
infographic.evidence_signal: On common successful random-circuit instances, mean two-qubit gate reductions range from 2.05% to 74.64% across three baselines; reported reductions on 4–6-qubit algorithm benchmarks range from 20.65% to 71.88%.
infographic.watch_item: Dynamic reconstruction applies only where terminal measurements are permitted, and gate-count savings alone do not establish hardware-level speed or fidelity gains.
infographic.paper_title: CAVQS: Context-Aware Variational Quantum Circuit Synthesis via Unitary Redistribution and Dynamic Reconstruction

title: Penalty-Free Constrained Optimization on Dynamic Quantum Circuits via Phase-Protected Tunneling and Closed-Loop Spectral Ratchets
authors: Chia-Ho Ou
abstract: Embedding hard operational constraints into an unconstrained Hamiltonian via large penalty multipliers induces quadratic spectral aliasing during phase estimation and increases two-qubit gate depth. This paper proposes a penalty-free, closed-loop dynamic quantum circuit scheme, designated as Zeno-decoupled gauge-ratchet optimization (Z-GRO), for constrained binary optimization without outer-loop training. Reversible feasibility phase operators within symmetric dynamical-decoupling echoes confine evolution to the feasible subspace, while an interaction-correlated commutator gauge operator resolves initial symmetry stall. Directional cooling couples the unpenalized objective Hamiltonian to a reusable ancilla with a zero-two-qubit-gate threshold offset, bypassing echoed tunneling gates on retained branches. A survival-filtered Ramsey controller advances the threshold from a linear-programming bound with automatic overshoot rollback. Exact density-matrix and trajectory simulations on spin-glass and quadratic knapsack ensembles show a single-check discrimination gain above four orders of magnitude, improving ground-state probability by factors of 3.0 to 4.3 over quantum Zeno dynamics and 11.4 to 22.5 over penalized schemes. Z-GRO reduces the spin-glass time-to-solution scaling base to 1.529 (compared to 1.684 for quantum Zeno dynamics and 1.909 to 2.047 for penalized schemes) and lowers 14-qubit knapsack time-to-solution by factors of 2.4 to 14.5. For two-qubit gate error rates between $5 \times 10^{-4}$ and $5 \times 10^{-3}$, Z-GRO achieves 2.9 to 7.0 times the optimal probability of noisy penalized feedback, while majority shielding limits loss to 6.3% at a 5.0% readout bit-flip rate, recording 0/24, 0/25, 0/96, 3/25, and 2/80 overshoots.

infographic.key_insight: Z-GRO avoids large constraint penalties by combining feasibility-protecting quantum evolution with closed-loop spectral cooling to favor feasible, low-cost solutions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The scheme targets constrained binary optimization on dynamic quantum circuits while reducing penalty-related spectral aliasing and two-qubit gate overhead.
method: Embed reversible feasibility phase operators in symmetric dynamical-decoupling echoes to protect the feasible subspace.
Use an interaction-correlated commutator gauge to overcome initial symmetry stall and ancilla-assisted cooling to favor lower objective values.

infographic.paper_title: Penalty-Free Constrained Optimization on Dynamic Quantum Circuits via Phase-Protected Tunneling and Closed-Loop Spectral Ratchets

title: Augmenting Quantum Neural Networks with Contractive Layers
authors: Bolin Huang, Pengfei Zhang
abstract: Classical neural networks combine diverse layers with complementary roles to achieve rich expressive capabilities across complex learning tasks. Rapid advances in quantum science and technology have motivated growing interest in their quantum counterparts, quantum neural networks, raising the question of how their expressivity can be enhanced through the design of new quantum layers. Of particular interest are layers that enrich the accessible function space while introducing only a small number of additional trainable parameters. In this Letter, we introduce the contractive layer as a promising building block for quantum neural networks. This layer comprises all-to-all couplings governed by a single trainable parameter, enabling efficient control of quantum information flow while maintaining experimental relevance to Rydberg atom arrays. Using observable learning as a benchmark, we show that contractive layers enhance expressivity more efficiently than simply increasing the depth of conventional brick-wall circuits. This advantage stems from a systematic increase in the accessible target-space dimension per trainable parameter. We further demonstrate similar improvements in image recognition tasks. These results highlight contractive layers as a practical route to expressive quantum neural networks on near-term quantum devices.

infographic.key_insight: Single-parameter contractive layers with all-to-all couplings improve quantum neural network expressivity more efficiently than adding conventional brick-wall circuit depth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Contractive layers offer a parameter-efficient design aligned with Rydberg atom arrays for enhancing near-term quantum neural networks.
method: Introduce all-to-all coupling layers governed by one trainable parameter.
Assess accessible target-space dimension per trainable parameter.
Benchmark against deeper brick-wall circuits on observable learning and image recognition.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved expressivity in observable learning and similar gains in image recognition, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical gains require validating all-to-all coupling fidelity and robustness to hardware noise, which the abstract does not quantify.
infographic.paper_title: Augmenting Quantum Neural Networks with Contractive Layers

title: Adaptive Hamiltonian Identification via Quantum Reinforcement Learning under Non-Stationary Dynamics
authors: Jawaher Kaldari, Saif Al-Kuwari
abstract: Accurate identification of the Hamiltonian governing a quantum system is important for quantum-system characterization, device calibration, simulation, and reliable operation of quantum hardware. In practical systems, however, the governing dynamics may vary over time because of parameter drift, changing control conditions, or transitions between operating regimes. In this work, we formulate Hamiltonian identification as a quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) problem in which a quantum agent processes sequential quantum-state observations and estimates the governing Hamiltonian parameters. We first consider stationary dynamics using a Vanilla-QRL agent and then introduce a recurrent GRU-QRL architecture to track non-stationary dynamics. The framework is evaluated on transverse-field Ising model systems under stationary dynamics, abrupt Hamiltonian switching, rapidly changing Hamiltonians, random switch locations over longer trajectories, and gradual Hamiltonian drift. We further compare the proposed approach with a Quantum Graph Recurrent Neural Network (QGRNN) baseline and evaluate frozen policies on unseen trajectories. Results show that both approaches accurately reconstruct stationary Hamiltonians, while GRU-QRL provides substantially improved tracking under non-stationary dynamics. These results demonstrate the potential of recurrent QRL as an adaptive system-identification tool for monitoring time-varying quantum systems.

infographic.key_insight: Recurrent quantum reinforcement learning improves tracking of time-varying Hamiltonians while retaining accurate identification under stationary dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive Hamiltonian estimation could support quantum-device calibration and monitoring when system parameters drift or operating regimes change.
method: Formulate Hamiltonian identification as reinforcement learning from sequential quantum-state observations.
Use Vanilla-QRL for stationary dynamics and recurrent GRU-QRL for non-stationary tracking.
Compare against a Quantum Graph Recurrent Neural Network baseline.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on transverse-field Ising systems cover stationary dynamics, abrupt and rapid switching, randomized switch locations, gradual drift, and frozen-policy tests on unseen trajectories.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish robustness to hardware noise or the measurement and computational costs of deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Hamiltonian Identification via Quantum Reinforcement Learning under Non-Stationary Dynamics

title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization
authors: Kasidit Srimahajariyapong, Thiparat Chotibut, Suwannachad Suwannajitt, Tithivich Paka, Ricard Puig, Yudai Suzuki
abstract: Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.

infographic.key_insight: Riemannian gradient updates enable autonomous quantum model training without measurements or classical feedback during optimization, under sufficient conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could remove the quantum–classical training bottleneck, with circuit-depth growth remaining a key implementation cost.
method: Derive quantum-domain Riemannian gradient updates for a broad class of learning tasks.
Identify sufficient conditions for fully autonomous training.
Prove exponential convergence in training iterations for sufficiently small step sizes within the autonomous regime.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical studies of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with hidden symmetry indicate successful learning at low circuit depths using few distinct training examples, including discovery of unspecified symmetries.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports numerical rather than hardware validation; practical feasibility depends on meeting the autonomy conditions and managing circuit-depth growth.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization

title: Full-chip constrained quantum annealing via self-calibrating spin-susceptibility control
authors: Chia-Ho Ou
abstract: Discrete optimization in finance, power grids, and logistics requires minimizing Ising Hamiltonians under coupled linear constraints. However, quadratic-penalty formulations generate dense cliques that exhaust the minor-embedding capacity of sparse superconducting processors at 128-176 spins, and first-order dual subgradient schemes diverge or stall under constraint coupling. Accordingly, this study proposes a closed-loop primal-dual scheme, designated as Self-Calibrating Quantum Susceptibility Quasi-Newton (SelfCal-QSQN), in which linear constraints are encoded in longitudinal fields and dual curvature is reconstructed from single-shot spin-fluctuation covariances. This scheme requires no penalty couplers, slack qubits, or perturbation queries. Evaluated over 891 runs on D-Wave Advantage (5,612 qubits) and Advantage2 (4,560 qubits), SelfCal-QSQN achieves 83.3% full-chip exact feasibility, reduces high-constraint error by 6.1-20.1-fold over $K$-scaled first-order updates (138.4-323.3-fold over fixed-gain curvature), outperforms time-matched mixed-integer programming at 256 spins, and attains 95.0%-96.7% feasibility on non-native and inequality benchmarks. Moreover, the scheme is robust toward shot noise and freeze-out drift.

infographic.key_insight: SelfCal-QSQN enforces coupled linear constraints through adaptive longitudinal fields, avoiding dense penalty couplers and enabling full-chip constrained quantum annealing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could expand usable problem sizes on sparse quantum annealers for constrained optimization in finance, power grids, and logistics.
method: Encode linear constraints in longitudinal fields using a closed-loop primal-dual scheme.
Estimate dual curvature from single-shot spin-fluctuation covariances.
Apply self-calibrating quasi-Newton updates without penalty couplers, slack qubits, or perturbation queries.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 891 runs on D-Wave Advantage and Advantage2, the study reports 83.3% full-chip exact feasibility, 6.1–20.1× lower high-constraint error than K-scaled first-order updates, and better performance than time-matched mixed-integer programming at 256 spins.
infographic.watch_item: Exact feasibility is not guaranteed, and the abstract does not establish broad end-to-end advantage over classical solvers beyond the reported benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: Full-chip constrained quantum annealing via self-calibrating spin-susceptibility control

title: Classical simulability and hardware diagnostics for QAOA on geographic coverage benchmarks
authors: F. S. Luiz, D Abreu, A. J. G. Abelém, J. E. Da Fonseca, A. F. P. Santos, M. C. de Oliveira
abstract: Quantum-optimization benchmarks can show reduced energy while concealing local loss of weighted covariance. We combine encoding checks with exact structural references to select informative circuit diagnostics for static geographic coverage instances. The executed 24-qubit surrogate has infeasible ground states, whereas a faithful 51-qubit slack encoding preserves its 13 support-graph components and remains exactly simulable blockwise. At the executed angles, the total ideal optimum probability is $5.47\times10^{-20}$, making optimum counts uninformative at the executed budget of $10^5$ shots. A product distribution with the measured bit marginals accounts for about $90\%$ of the observed energy reduction. In three fixed-circuit jobs, the global weighted-covariance ratio is approximately $0.50$, while a five-variable block has ratios between $0.12$ and $0.28$ and contributes only $3.7\%$ of the ideal global denominator. Simultaneous bands resolve its deficit relative to the global ratio under an exploratory conditional counting model. The exact block reference thus reveals a local discrepancy concealed by the aggregate, without identifying an error mechanism or establishing device stability. The procedure links benchmark structure to the resolution and limitations of its observables.

infographic.key_insight: Exact blockwise references reveal local covariance loss in QAOA hardware results that aggregate energy improvements can conceal.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Check encoding feasibility and benchmark structure before choosing hardware diagnostics, since lower energy alone can overstate useful circuit performance.
method: Compare the executed 24-qubit surrogate with a faithful 51-qubit slack encoding.
Exploit 13 support-graph components for exact blockwise simulation.
Compare measured weighted covariance with ideal references and a product-distribution baseline.

infographic.paper_title: Classical simulability and hardware diagnostics for QAOA on geographic coverage benchmarks

title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities
authors: Q. Rumman Rahman, S. M. Girvin, D. K. Weiss
abstract: The realization of large-scale quantum computation will require quantum error correction (QEC). One way to reduce the demands placed on QEC is to correct dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing the remaining errors to an outer code. Recently, Krastanov et al. [Nat. Commun. 12, 191 (2021)] proposed a measurement-free error-correction protocol based on coherent control of photonic modes that corrects for photon loss. Here, we adapt this approach to a circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. We encode the logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one cavity, while the two other cavities serve as ancillas. Using numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters, we demonstrate that our protocol can correct single-photon loss with 99% fidelity. Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: A simulated measurement-free protocol corrects single-photon loss in superconducting cavities and extends logical-qubit lifetime beyond an unprotected Fock encoding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coherent, gate-based correction of photon loss could reduce the error burden passed to an outer quantum error-correcting code.
method: Encode a logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one microwave cavity.
Use two ancillary cavities and Josephson-junction-based nonlinear couplings for measurement-free correction.
Optimize the waiting time between successive correction rounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters report 99% single-photon-loss correction fidelity and a 1.2–1.8× logical-lifetime gain over unprotected {|0⟩, |1⟩} Fock encoding.
infographic.watch_item: The reported gains are simulation-based; experimental performance will depend on achieving sufficiently accurate coherent control and cavity couplings.
infographic.paper_title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities

title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction
authors: Chenyang Jin, Susanne F. Yelin, Andi Gu
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires a classical decoder fast enough to process syndrome measurements at the rate at which they are generated, and to return its decisions with low latency. This is most demanding for superconducting processors, whose fast syndrome cycles force a trade-off between decoding speed and accuracy. Decoders fast enough to keep up sacrifice accuracy, which must be compensated for with larger codes and thus additional physical qubits. Here we introduce Rapids, a streaming neural decoder that is both fast and accurate. We achieve this by co-designing the decoder with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA): the network is built from operations that map cheaply onto the device and trained in its integer arithmetic. For the distance-19 surface code, Rapids decodes each round of syndromes in under a microsecond on a single FPGA, fast enough for superconducting processors, and returns its decisions with the low latency that fault-tolerant algorithms require. Its logical error rate is 240 times lower than that of existing real-time hardware decoders. The same design extends to the color code and the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code, on which our decoder is 16 times more accurate than the real-time Relay decoder. We further show that the decoder scales: spread over several FPGAs or hardened into custom silicon, it becomes faster, more accurate, or able to decode larger codes. Classical hardware thus becomes a further resource, alongside qubits, that can be scaled to improve fault-tolerant quantum computers.

infographic.key_insight: Rapids co-designs a streaming neural decoder with FPGA hardware to deliver fast, accurate real-time quantum error correction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Scaling classical decoding hardware alongside qubits offers a route to improving fault-tolerant quantum computers without sacrificing decoding accuracy for speed.
method: Use neural-network operations that map efficiently onto FPGAs.
Train the decoder in the hardware’s integer arithmetic.
Scale across multiple FPGAs or implement the design in custom silicon.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports under 1 microsecond per syndrome round for a distance-19 surface code on one FPGA, a 240-fold lower logical error rate than existing real-time hardware decoders, and 16-fold better accuracy than Relay on the [[144,12,12]] bivariate-bicycle code.
infographic.watch_item: Sub-microsecond processing per round does not alone establish end-to-end control latency; deployment must account for data transfer and decoder integration.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling classical hardware for accurate real-time quantum error correction

title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
authors: Stefano Tinelli, Francisco Lázaro, Francisco García Herrero
abstract: A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.

infographic.key_insight: Non-binary detector error models preserve Pauli fault distributions exactly while enabling smaller decoding graphs and better belief-propagation performance than binary models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tanner graphs with 4–5× fewer edges can reduce decoder connectivity demands, while BP with OSD achieved up to 9.4× CPU speedup.
method: Represent each circuit fault location as one random variable over its original Pauli-error alphabet.
Use split-merge-regroup to compact Clifford-circuit models by merging components with identical detector and observable effects.
Decode using belief propagation with one scalar message per edge, optionally followed by OSD.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical evaluations on surface, color, and bivariate bicycle codes report better BP performance with and without OSD, fewer graph edges, and faster CPU decoding.
infographic.watch_item: The reported speedup is a best-case CPU result; hardware latency and resource savings require implementation-specific validation.
infographic.paper_title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models

title: QFT-Based Hybrid PointNet-Quantum Neural Networks for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification
authors: Anurag Kulkarni, Nouhaila Innan, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical learning architectures provide a promising framework for integrating quantum feature transformations into complex data-processing tasks. Among these transformations, the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) offers a structured approach to feature processing, motivating an investigation of how its circuit configuration influences predictive performance, quantum resource requirements, and noise robustness. We present a hybrid PointNet-quantum neural network architecture for LiDAR point-cloud classification, combining classical feature extraction, amplitude encoding, and a variational quantum circuit. Five Fourier-processing configurations are systematically evaluated: No-QFT, Full-QFT-After, QFT-no-swap, IQFT-After, and Trainable-QFT. Experiments on KITTI, nuScenes, and PandaSet across three random seeds assess classification performance, class-level behavior, circuit complexity, and sensitivity to the IBM FakeManilaV2 noise model. Under ideal simulation, IQFT-After achieves the highest weighted F1-score on KITTI (0.857 $\pm$ 0.033), compared with 0.838 $\pm$ 0.023 for No-QFT. Removing the final SWAP gates in the QFT circuit reduces circuit complexity while preserving the Pauli-Z measurement features up to a fixed permutation that can be absorbed by the classification head. Under quantum noise, the circuit ranking changes, with IQFT-After exhibiting greater performance degradation and No-QFT and Trainable-QFT showing stronger robustness. Per-class analysis further identifies dataset-dependent differences in minority-class performance. These results demonstrate that Fourier-processing configuration influences both classification behavior and noise sensitivity, highlighting the role of circuit structure and hardware-aware evaluation in hybrid quantum learning for three-dimensional point-cloud data.

infographic.key_insight: Fourier-circuit configuration affects both LiDAR classification accuracy and noise sensitivity: IQFT-After performs best on ideal KITTI simulations, while No-QFT and Trainable-QFT are more robust under noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hardware-aware circuit selection can balance predictive performance, quantum resource requirements, and noise robustness in hybrid point-cloud classifiers.
method: Combine PointNet feature extraction, amplitude encoding, and a variational quantum circuit.
Compare No-QFT, Full-QFT-After, QFT-no-swap, IQFT-After, and Trainable-QFT.
Remove final QFT SWAP gates to reduce complexity while preserving Pauli-Z features up to a fixed permutation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on KITTI, nuScenes, and PandaSet across three seeds includes IBM FakeManilaV2 noise simulations; ideal KITTI weighted F1 is 0.857 ± 0.033 for IQFT-After versus 0.838 ± 0.023 for No-QFT.
infographic.watch_item: Noise-model simulations do not establish real-hardware performance, and the best ideal-simulation circuit may not remain best under noise.
infographic.paper_title: QFT-Based Hybrid PointNet-Quantum Neural Networks for LiDAR Point-Cloud Classification

title: The classical complexity of quantum state transmission
authors: Elna Svegborn, Alexander Bernal, Armin Tavakoli
abstract: Quantum communication provides a natural means to transmit quantum information, but how difficult is it to make such a transmission using only classical communication resources? We address this question by introducing classical communication models for quantum preparations and defining their minimum cost as the classical complexity. We prove that this complexity equals the amount of classical communication required to simulate quantum correlations in prepare-and-broadcast experiments, thus establishing a resource equivalence between quantum state transmission and quantum correlations. This calls for a general characterisation of the classical complexity of the noisy quantum state space, which we show grows exponentially with the quantum dimension and as a power-law in the inverse noise. It reveals the rapidly scaling fundamental cost of classical simulation. Moreover, we develop a toolbox of methods to certify classical complexity in quantum preparation devices, including an exact semidefinite-programming characterisation, analytical witnesses for symmetric preparations and convex programming scalable up to hundreds and sometimes thousands of qubit states. Our results establish classical complexity as a fundamental measure of quantum communication advantage, revealing the intrinsic cost of classically simulating quantum theory and providing practical tools for its certification.

infographic.key_insight: The classical communication cost of simulating quantum state transmission equals that of simulating prepare-and-broadcast quantum correlations and grows exponentially with quantum dimension.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Classical complexity offers a resource benchmark for quantum communication advantage and tools to certify quantum preparation devices.
method: Define minimum-cost classical communication models for quantum preparations.
Prove resource equivalence with prepare-and-broadcast correlation simulation.
Certify complexity using semidefinite programming, analytical witnesses and scalable convex programming.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical scaling exponential in quantum dimension and power-law in inverse noise, plus convex-programming methods handling hundreds and sometimes thousands of qubit states.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report hardware validation, and practical certification costs may depend on the preparation set and optimization method.
infographic.paper_title: The classical complexity of quantum state transmission

title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Anastasiia Lukianenko, Yash J. Patel, Nurbolat Kenbayev, Vedran Dunjko
abstract: Quantum error mitigation (QEM) can recover information about ideal quantum computations from noisy circuit executions, but may require a large sampling overhead. Fundamental lower bounds show that recovering noiseless observables without problem-specific information can require superpolynomially many samples, with exponential overhead for broad classes of noisy circuits. However, problem-specific information can reduce the number of samples needed to obtain the required answer. We investigate this possibility in supervised quantum machine learning, where labeled examples provide information about the function to be learned. Binary classification provides such a setting, since correct prediction depends on the sign and margin of the classifier output rather than on accurate reconstruction of every noiseless expectation value. We develop a theoretical and empirical framework for comparing boosting of noisy parameterized quantum circuits with probabilistic error cancellation (PEC), requiring both methods to reach the same learning target. For the specified circuit architectures under Pauli noise, we establish a common hypothesis-class complexity bound: matching empirical margin loss gives the same upper bound on expected classification risk. We derive resource criteria and evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost in finite-shot teacher-student simulations across circuit depth and physical noise strength. Under the same classification-accuracy target, boosting requires fewer circuit executions as depth and noise increase. Boosting also achieves higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference. For the supervised-learning problems studied, these results demonstrate a task-dependent resource advantage: exploiting information retained in noisy outputs can avoid the cost of ideal-output reconstruction without sacrificing observed classification performance.

infographic.key_insight: Boosting noisy quantum classifiers can reach the same classification target as probabilistic error cancellation with fewer circuit executions, without reconstructing ideal outputs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For supervised quantum learning, optimizing classification performance directly may reduce sampling costs compared with correcting noisy expectation values.
method: Compare boosted noisy parameterized quantum circuits with probabilistic error cancellation at a matched learning target.
Establish a shared classification-risk upper bound when empirical margin loss is matched for the specified architectures under Pauli noise.
Evaluate AdaBoostR and Real AdaBoost in finite-shot teacher–student simulations across circuit depth and noise strength.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations show fewer circuit executions for boosting at matched classification accuracy as depth and noise increase, plus higher test accuracy than the corresponding reference.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstrated advantage is task-dependent and based on specified architectures and simulated noise, not a general hardware guarantee.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Error Mitigation: Using Boosting for Noisy Quantum Machine Learning

title: Optimised 8th-Order Trotter-Suzuki Schemes for Quantum Simulation
authors: Marko Maležič, Johann Ostmeyer
abstract: Simulating quantum dynamics in many-body systems is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers. Product formulas are a natural choice for this task, since they map directly onto quantum gates, and increasing their order $n$ could lead to reduced gate depths, provided the parameters are chosen efficiently. So far, schemes beyond $6^{\textrm{th}}$ order have only been built as compositions of second-order schemes, while more general product formulas are known only up to $6^{\textrm{th}}$ order. In this work, we extend our optimisation framework to order $n = 8$, and find both more efficient compositions and the first $8^{\textrm{th}}$ order general schemes. Our formulas improve on the theoretical efficiency of the state-of-the-art schemes by Morales et al and we recommend two schemes explicitly. In simulations of the Heisenberg XZ chain one of our recommended schemes always outperforms those by Morales et al, though it is not always the same scheme that performs best. More generally, we observe that for Hamiltonians split into many non-commuting operators the uniformity of a Trotter decomposition becomes the main indicator of a scheme's performance. To assess the schemes' use on quantum hardware, we simulate noisy circuits with our new Qiskit plugin qiskit-omelyan. At current noise levels, the Leapfrog scheme remains the best choice, but as noise rates decrease toward fault tolerance, our recommended schemes become competitive.

infographic.key_insight: Optimised eighth-order Trotter–Suzuki formulas improve theoretical quantum-simulation efficiency, including the first general schemes at this order.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These formulas could reduce gate-depth requirements as hardware noise decreases, while second-order Leapfrog remains preferable at current noise levels.
method: Extend product-formula optimisation to eighth order.
Develop improved compositions and general eighth-order schemes.
Evaluate Heisenberg XZ-chain dynamics and noisy circuits using qiskit-omelyan.
infographic.evidence_signal: In Heisenberg XZ-chain simulations, at least one of the two recommended schemes consistently outperforms the Morales et al. benchmarks, though the best-performing scheme varies.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on hardware noise and Hamiltonian splitting; for many non-commuting terms, decomposition uniformity becomes a key indicator.
infographic.paper_title: Optimised 8th-Order Trotter-Suzuki Schemes for Quantum Simulation

title: Single-realization Pauli twirling for suppressing coherent error accumulation in structured quantum circuits
authors: Dihang Sun, Tianqi Chen, Jin Ming Koh, Nannan Ma, Jiangbin Gong
abstract: Pauli twirling is conventionally understood as an ensemble-level noise-tailoring procedure which suppresses coherent components of the error channel by averaging over randomized compilations. This picture does not by itself determine whether a single realization of Pauli-dressed circuit can outperform its bare counterpart, nor does it predict when such an advantage should occur. In this work, we present single-realization based framework for the standard Pauli dressing of two-qubit Clifford gates in structured quantum circuits. This is afforded by the key insight that for weak coherent errors, the leading gate infidelity is governed by the variance of some accumulated error generator. Through both simulations and theoretical considerations, we verify that coherent errors accumulated at different entangling gates can produce $Θ(L^2)$ variance growth in a bare circuit, whereas independent Pauli dressing eliminates the cross-layer contribution on average and yields an $O(L)$ variance bound at any fixed confidence level for a single randomly sampled realization. We then develop a covariance diagnostic that predicts when this mechanism is effective in error mitigation. We find a strong Pauli twirling advantage for coherent errors whose transported generators have large off-diagonal covariance, and little advantage when the covariance matrix is nearly diagonal. Hardware experiments on IBM superconducting processors demonstrate fidelity improvements for GHZ-state preparation and reduced observable errors in Trotterized transverse-field Ising dynamics. These results indicate that single realizations of Pauli twirling without ensemble averaging is a useful coherent-error suppression technique for structured circuits containing repeated nontrivial two-qubit operations.

infographic.key_insight: A single randomly Pauli-dressed circuit can suppress coherent error accumulation when correlations between transported error generators would otherwise amplify it.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For structured quantum circuits, Pauli dressing can improve fidelity without averaging over multiple randomized circuit compilations.
method: Relate leading infidelity under weak coherent errors to accumulated error-generator variance.
Independently Pauli-dress two-qubit Clifford gates to remove cross-layer contributions on average.
Use a covariance diagnostic to predict when dressing is beneficial.
infographic.evidence_signal: Theory and simulations show possible quadratic variance growth in bare circuits versus a linear bound at fixed confidence for one random dressed realization; IBM hardware experiments demonstrate improved GHZ fidelity and reduced observable errors in Trotterized transverse-field Ising dynamics.
infographic.watch_item: The analysis assumes weak coherent errors, and little benefit is expected when the transported-generator covariance matrix is nearly diagonal.
infographic.paper_title: Single-realization Pauli twirling for suppressing coherent error accumulation in structured quantum circuits

title: Beyond the Stabilizer Norm: Physicality and Resource Allocation in Pauli-Limited Quantum Certification
authors: Shreya Savadatti, Peter Yun Zhang
abstract: Certification from restricted and uncertain Pauli measurements can be posed as a robust optimization problem: among all physical channels consistent with the data, how small can the fidelity with a target channel be? We first study a linear relaxation that ignores positivity and show that it is exactly characterized by a single scalar, the stabilizer norm of the target Choi state, $s_{\mathrm{wit}}(U)=\|C_U\|_{\mathrm{st}}-1/D$. We then ask whether this scalar continues to determine robustness once the positivity constraint is restored. It does not. We derive a necessary and sufficient KKT condition for the relaxation to remain tight, together with a dual obstruction certifying a strict gap, and give a rigorous computer-assisted proof that two distinct two-qubit targets can have exactly the same stabilizer norm but different physical robustness. The KKT condition depends on structure discarded by the stabilizer norm, including the support and relative signs of the Choi-Pauli coefficients and the algebraic relations among the corresponding Pauli operators. We use this structure to derive simpler sufficient certificates for a strict gap. The dual coefficients also determine how measurement uncertainty enters the finite-data fidelity bound. For a fixed budget, we derive exact shot-allocation rules for a fixed certificate and for compatible observables obtained from shared measurement settings, and we formulate the corresponding joint certificate-design problem. The conjecture that every full-support two-qubit target has positive gain remains open.

infographic.key_insight: The stabilizer norm alone cannot determine robustness in Pauli-limited quantum certification: physical channel constraints make the target’s operator structure matter.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Dual certificates quantify how measurement uncertainty affects fidelity bounds and guide shot allocation under a fixed measurement budget.
method: Characterize the positivity-free relaxation exactly using the target Choi state’s stabilizer norm.
Derive a necessary and sufficient KKT tightness condition and dual certificates for strict physicality gaps.
Derive exact shot-allocation rules for fixed certificates, including compatible observables sharing measurement settings.
infographic.evidence_signal: A rigorous computer-assisted proof establishes two distinct two-qubit targets with exactly equal stabilizer norm but different physical robustness.
infographic.watch_item: Whether every full-support two-qubit target has positive gain from enforcing physicality remains open.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond the Stabilizer Norm: Physicality and Resource Allocation in Pauli-Limited Quantum Certification

title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
authors: Joshua Aftergood, Daniele Guerci, Jacob Brunton, Feng Zhang, Thomas Iadecola, Peter P. Orth
abstract: Simulating the real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires a nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, a challenge for classical methods. We present the time-dependent Gutzwiller quantum-classical embedding framework, t-GQCE, for generic multi-orbital lattice models with time-dependent Hamiltonians. Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice dynamics is mapped onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice, propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models propagated on quantum processors. The two parts exchange only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices, and the framework is agnostic to the quantum dynamics solver. We demonstrate it with adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice. Without ghost orbitals, the embedding problem reduces to a single qubit, simulated on IBM quantum hardware with two qubits, including an ancilla. With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses the artificial undamped oscillations of the conventional Gutzwiller approximation and approaches nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results for weak and strong quenches. Statevector simulations with 2, 4 and 6 ghost orbitals per spin, or 8, 12 and 16 qubits, give adaptive circuits that follow the embedding states with infidelities below $5\times10^{-4}$. Under trapped-ion noise models, circuit compression, measurements in rotated orbital bases with post-selection, and noise mitigation reduce the measurement errors severalfold. At one third of the error rates of a hardware-benchmarked noise model, they reach an accuracy of $0.01$ for the single-particle density matrix and the double occupancy with $10^5$ shots per time step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator gives similar accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: t-GQCE couples classical lattice dynamics to quantum embedding models, with added ghost orbitals improving correlated-electron dynamics toward nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework assigns noninteracting lattice propagation to classical computers and finite interacting models to quantum processors, exchanging only Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices.
method: Map time-dependent multi-orbital lattices into classical quasiparticles coupled to quantum embedding models.
Propagate embedding states with adaptive variational quantum dynamics, while remaining compatible with other quantum solvers.
Reduce noise using circuit compression, rotated-orbital measurements, post-selection, and mitigation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Hubbard-quench statevector tests used 8–16 qubits with infidelities below 5×10⁻⁴; reduced-noise simulations reached 0.01 accuracy for density matrices and double occupancy at 10⁵ shots per time step, with similar accuracy on the Quantinuum H2-Emulator.
infographic.watch_item: Larger demonstrations rely on simulation or emulation; the reported reduced-noise accuracy requires one-third of hardware-benchmarked error rates and substantial measurement sampling.
infographic.paper_title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
